gaps.fact: Southwest France placed south of Bordeaux and north of the Languedoc against the Pyrenees, and the Dordogne flowing west from the Massif Central through Bergerac: there is no Southwest article, and the Codex places Bergerac only as the land east of Saint-Émilion.
Provence makes nearly 90 per cent dry rosé: the article says mostly rosé and gives no share.
Côtes de Provence AOP, its four grapes and its rosé dominance: the Village bank asks Cassis, Palette, Bellet and Bandol but no question asks the grapes or the style of Côtes de Provence itself.

Limoux AOP red as a Merlot dominant dry red, and Crémant de Limoux's Mauzac and Pinot Noir with its rosé: the Codex says only that Limoux makes still red and that the Crémant is led by Chardonnay and Chenin Blanc.

The partner grapes and the red only rule: Merlot and Tannat beside Côt in Cahors, Cabernet Franc and Cabernet Sauvignon beside Tannat in Madiran, both dry red only; the chapter gives the lead grape of each and nothing more, and no question asks either appellation outside a pairing.

Bergerac AOP's own grape lists: Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Sauvignon Gris and Muscadelle for the dry white; Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Côt and Merlot for red and rosé. The Codex says only that the Bordeaux grapes cross the line, and Sauvignon Gris is named nowhere.

The Banyuls producers the Court names, Chapoutier and Domaine du Mas Blanc: neither is linked to Banyuls anywhere in the Codex (Chapoutier appears only in the Rhône); and the three Bandol estates are asked in no question.

Provence as the birthplace of wine in France, making wine since 600 BCE, and the Southwest growing grapes since 125 BC: the first is a clause in the France sheet's overview, the second appears nowhere, and no question asks either.

Monbazillac with fruit desserts, foie gras and salty or creamy cheeses; Banyuls with figs, foie gras and salty blue cheese; Provence rosé with shellfish and bouillabaisse: none is asked, and Monbazillac is paired nowhere in the Codex.

notes: Mapped questions: Régionale 0 (no category), Village 21 (Southern France), 21 in all. Beyond the map the subject is asked in seven other categories: Sweet Wines 12 (Jurançon, Pacherenc, Monbazillac, Saussignac, the Bergerac sweet belt), Fortified Wines 5 (Banyuls, Rivesaltes, Maury, cartagène), Dessert & Sweet Wines 3, Sparkling/Fortified/Sweet 2, Grapes & Labels 4, Geography & Maps 3 and Food & Pairing 1, about 30 more in all. The Provence and Languedoc columns are well served on appellations, crus, Bandol's rules, Limoux's history and the Vins Doux Naturels; the thin cells are the Southwest and Dordogne columns, which have no article and rest on one chapter fact each and the Sweet Wines stems, the partner grapes of Cahors and Madiran, the Limoux red, the Banyuls producers, the two History lines and the pairings. No factual error found: Bandol's 50 per cent Mourvèdre and eighteen months in wood, Fitou 1948, La Livinière 1999, Boutenac 2005, Terrasses du Larzac 2014, Banyuls Grand Cru's 30 months, hors d'âge at five years, Cahors at 70 per cent Côt and the mutage dose all hold. Two readings to carry: the Court prints Continental for Southwest France and the Dordogne, where the Codex's climate card files the South West as Atlantic; and the Court calls plain Jurançon off-dry, where the chapter and c-pdajp9y9 teach it as the moelleux; give the Court's words on the paper. One search spent, on Cahors: nothing in the Court's southern appellations has moved since 8.2023; the 2024 renaming of La Livinière and Boutenac and the Montpeyroux approval of 2025 fall outside the Court's cells and are already in the article.
